$comment: What each surface of each corpus measures, and the NULL it is held to: the same estimator over the same features with the labels shuffled, which is what that surface produces when it carries no information at all. Written by scripts/surface-leakage-gate.py --sync and enforced by the same script with no argument. A figure above its recorded `separability` refuses, whether or not it is outside its null. A figure outside its `null` is a regularity shuffling does not reproduce, and refuses unless the row names the constraint blocking it; a row naming one after coming back inside its null refuses as a stale declaration. `fingerprint` is the class counts the null was calibrated over, because those set its level. Do not raise a number here to quiet the gate.

identifier.blockedBy: the published identifier namespace, filename and directory both
identifier.reason: A PERFECT predictor on both corpora, measured over the vector's whole manifest-relative path: the `ok-`/`bad-` prefix and the `accept/`/`reject/` directory each name the label outright, and either alone is enough. The fix is to content-address the identifier AND flatten the corpus into one directory, retiring every old identifier permanently. GOVERNANCE.md's commitment is that an identifier is never REUSED, which a permanent retirement honours, so nothing in it blocks this. The gate's own test performs the substitution, so the outcome is measured rather than argued: this surface falls to 0.5075 on the larger corpus and 0.5245 on the smaller, both well inside their nulls.

all.blockedBy: the published identifier namespace, filename and directory both
all.reason: Carried by the identifier surface above and by nothing else. Every other surface of this corpus is inside its own null, so once the identifier is content-addressed and the corpus flattened this figure is 0.5568 against a null of 0.5836: statistically indistinguishable from a corpus carrying no leakage at all.

paths.blockedBy: the Appendix B family having no reject counterpart
paths.reason: Real, and outside the null by a wide margin rather than by a hair. The accept side carries `predicate.contentDigest` on 26 of its 37 members and the reject side on 1 of 16, because 24 of the accepts are the RFC 8785 Appendix B number-serialization family, generated in one loop, with no reject counterpart at all. The presence of one member path therefore very nearly names the label. This is the leak that survives the identifier fix: with identifiers content-addressed and the corpus flattened this corpus still measures 0.7780 against a null of 0.6716. The fix is on the reject side, Appendix B rows that serialize the number wrongly built from the same template, and it is corpus authorship rather than anything a gate can do.

lexicon.blockedBy: the Appendix B family having no reject counterpart
lexicon.reason: The member names and the shared digest string of the same Appendix B family described in the paths row. One string value appears in 25 of the 37 accept vectors and in no reject vector.

all.blockedBy: the Appendix B family having no reject counterpart, over the published identifier namespace, filename and directory both
all.reason: Both causes at once, and unlike the other corpus this one leaks through its content on its own, so the identifier fix does not take it inside its null.
